scenario.description: Billing dispute tickets roughly doubled in August-September. Customer Service wants an AI agent. Field reading is contracted out; AMI meters and the meter data management system (MDMS) are run by a vendor.

CL-01.statement: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

CL-02.statement: There has been no tariff change this year.

H-RESPONSE-SPEED.statement: The dispute surge is primarily a ticket-handling capacity/response-speed problem, so an AI agent that auto-answers CRM tickets would resolve it (SH-CS framing).

H-RULE-CHANGE-DEFECT.statement: A change to billing import validation rules (DA-RULES) around August introduced incorrect bill calculations or wrong estimate substitution, directly causing the dispute surge.

H-AMI-READ-DELIVERY-FAILURE.statement: AMI register reads from the vendor (ORG-AMI, via H-MDMS-BILL nightly export) are failing to deliver or validate, forcing more bills onto estimates and causing inaccuracies since August.

H-FIELD-READ-FAILURE.statement: Manual meter read collection by the contracted field service (ORG-FIELD, via H-FIELD-BILL daily upload) is incomplete or delayed, increasing estimate substitution and billing errors.

H-TICKET-REPORTING-ARTIFACT.statement: The apparent doubling of dispute tickets is a measurement/categorization artifact in CRM reporting (e.g., changed ticket tagging) rather than a real increase in billing errors.

H-FIELD-STAFFING-SHORTAGE.statement: A reduction of three field readers since July has caused routes to run late, increasing estimate substitution for the affected manual-read customers.

interpretation_history.interpretation: CRM dispute volume was ~600/month in Jun-Jul 2026 and jumped to ~1180-1260/month in Aug-Sep 2026, confirming the raw magnitude of the surge (roughly doubled). The record quantifies the symptom only; it says nothing about which upstream cause (AMI, field reads, billing rules, ticket miscategorization, or response speed) is responsible.

CRM response-time data (2440 tickets) shows median response of 1.6 days and p90 of 2.8 days, both within the 3.0-day SLA. This indicates ticket handling is currently meeting its response-time target, so slow response/capacity is not the mechanism driving the dispute surge; it says nothing about why bills are being disputed in the first place.

Billing-db shows 3,025 CRM-disputed bills split by read type: 1,240 ESTIMATED and 1,785 ACTUAL. Disputed bills are not concentrated on estimated reads — a majority (59%) carry an ACTUAL read, so disputes are not confined to bills produced via estimate substitution. Without the base split of ACTUAL vs ESTIMATED across all bills (not just disputed ones), this cannot yet show whether estimates are over- or under-represented relative to their normal share.

The billing-db tariff_change_log shows zero records, meaning no tariff/pricing changes were logged that could explain altered bill amounts since August. This rules out tariff revision as an alternative cause of the dispute surge, but does not speak to AMI, field-read, or import-rule causes.

Field route completion for Aug-Sep 2026 was 0.88 against a 0.95 target across 9,200 manual-read accounts, indicating a measurable shortfall in manual meter-read collection during the surge period. This is a direct completeness gap in the field-read channel (H-FIELD-BILL), not yet tied to the AMI/vendor channel or billing rules.

E-06.content: There has been no tariff change this year.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-BILL (Billing Operations Lead) states no tariff change occurred this year, which corroborates the already-recorded authoritative tool finding (E-04, tariff_change_log=0 records) ruling out a tariff change since August. As a stakeholder claim it is non-authoritative and adds no new causal information about AMI, field reads, or import rules.

E-07.content: We are short three readers since July; routes run late, so those customers get estimated bills.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-FIELD claims routes run late because the field service has been short three readers since July, and those late-read customers get estimated bills. This is an unverified stakeholder claim (not a tool record) offering a candidate mechanism behind the route-completion shortfall already seen in E-05, but SH-FIELD has a stated incentive to push for headcount and a bias toward staffing attributions.

E-08.content: Service contract §4.2: utility may request route priority changes; executed after Field Operations Manager confirmation.

interpretation_history.interpretation: The document confirms the contractual basis for K-DISPATCH: route priority changes requested by the utility are only executed after the Field Operations Manager (SH-FIELD) confirms them at runtime; it addresses authorization procedure, not the cause of the dispute surge.

E-09.content: route-log.lagging_routes → 14 record(s); fields ['completion', 'route'] | completion: 14 distinct values | route: 14 distinct values | sample: {"completion": 0.7, "route": "R-00"}

interpretation_history.interpretation: route-log.lagging_routes (E-09) breaks the aggregate 0.88 completion figure (E-05) down into 14 individual routes, each with its own completion value (sample: route R-00 at 0.7), confirming route-level variation in the shortfall. It does not include any account/bill identifiers, so it cannot by itself show whether these 14 lagging routes correspond to the 1,240 ESTIMATED disputed bills.

E-10.content: billing-db.accounts_estimated_last_cycle → 320 record(s); fields ['account_id', 'route'] | account_id: 320 distinct values | route: 40 distinct values | sample: {"account_id": "AC-20000", "route": "R-00"}

interpretation_history.interpretation: billing-db.accounts_estimated_last_cycle (E-10) returns 320 accounts billed on estimated reads in the most recent cycle, spread across 40 distinct field routes, with only account_id and route fields (no read_type, tariff, dispute, or import-status fields as the W-WI-BILL description anticipated).
